job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

passage: In our history workshop today, we explored how the Bhakti and Sufi movements challenged rigid social structures. We learned that the Virashaiva movement, led by Basavanna in Karnataka, rejected temple worship and elaborate rituals, arguing instead for direct devotion to Shiva. Unlike the traditional view that religious leadership was restricted to the upper castes, the Bhakti movement saw saints emerging from diverse backgrounds, including artisans and women like Mirabai, who dedicated her life to Krishna rather than seeking royal power. We also examined the Sufi tradition, which originated in the Islamic world. A central feature of Sufi life was the Khanqah, a hospice where Sufi masters held discussions and provided shelter to people of all faiths, emphasizing a shared mysticism rather than a separate religion. Furthermore, we studied Kabir, a poet-saint who boldly criticized the empty rituals and dogmas found in both Hindu and Islamic traditions. Finally, we clarified that the Bhakti movement actually began in South India with the Nayanars, who were devotees of Shiva, and the Alvars, who worshipped Vishnu, before spreading northwards. These movements collectively promoted equality and personal connection with the divine, transcending the boundaries of caste, gender, and formal religious institutions.

items.evidence: We learned that the Virashaiva movement, led by Basavanna in Karnataka, rejected temple worship and elaborate rituals, arguing instead for direct devotion to Shiva.
items.q: A Virashaiva devotee skips the village temple and prays to Shiva at home. Why?
options: Devotion to Shiva needs no temple or ritual
Temples were open only to the upper castes
Basavanna asked followers to build grand temples
Shiva could be worshipped only in Karnataka
items.explain: Virashaivas rejected temple worship and rituals, favouring direct devotion to Shiva.

wrong.why: thinks the issue was only caste access to temples
turns the place of the movement into a rule

items.evidence: Unlike the traditional view that religious leadership was restricted to the upper castes, the Bhakti movement saw saints emerging from diverse backgrounds, including artisans and women like Mirabai, who dedicated her life to Krishna rather than seeking royal power.
items.q: Which example shows that Bhakti leadership was not limited to upper castes?
options: Saints who came from artisan families
Saints who were all born as Brahmins
Saints who were chosen by the kings
Saints who ruled as queens in palaces
items.explain: Bhakti saints came from diverse backgrounds, including artisans and women, so leadership was not restricted to upper castes.

wrong.why: thinks Bhakti leaders were only Brahmins
thinks kings decided who became a saint
thinks Mirabai wanted to be a queen

items.evidence: A central feature of Sufi life was the Khanqah, a hospice where Sufi masters held discussions and provided shelter to people of all faiths, emphasizing a shared mysticism rather than a separate religion.
items.q: How was a Khanqah different from an ordinary inn for travellers?
options: Masters held talks there and welcomed all faiths
Only Muslim travellers could stay there overnight
Rich merchants paid to rest there for a night
Musicians played there for the royal family
items.explain: A Khanqah was a hospice where Sufi masters held discussions and sheltered people of all faiths.

wrong.why: thinks Sufis and their places were closed to others
thinks a Khanqah was just a paid hotel
links Sufi places only with music

items.evidence: Finally, we clarified that the Bhakti movement actually began in South India with the Nayanars, who were devotees of Shiva, and the Alvars, who worshipped Vishnu, before spreading northwards.
items.q: A poet-saint of the Alvars sings in praise of a god. Which god is it?
options: Krishna, but never Vishnu in any form
Basavanna, the leader of the Alvars
items.explain: The Alvars worshipped Vishnu, while the Nayanars were devotees of Shiva.

wrong.why: swaps the Nayanars and the Alvars
picks Krishna, a name nearby in the passage
mixes up a leader with a god
